info.bio:
Daphne Oram (31 de diciembre de 1925 – 5 de enero de 2003), fue una compositora y música electrónica de origen inglés. Creadora de la técnica "Oramics", la cual es usada para crear sonidos electrónicos.

Estudió en el Sherborne School For Girls. Desde temprana edad Oram aprendió el piano, el órgano y composición musical.1 En 1942 le ofrecieron una plaza en el Royal College of Music; sin embargo, rechazó esta propuesta y aceptó una posición en la BBC como ingeniera de estudio y también encargada del balance tonal de la música.

podcast.title: BBC Junior Studio Engineer (1942)
podcast.body: In 1942, Daphne Oram began her career as a junior studio engineer at the BBC. Her initial responsibility was to ensure uninterrupted music broadcasts during Nazi bombing raids by seamlessly switching to recorded music if live transmissions were disrupted, serving as a morale booster and a psychological tactic against the enemy. "In 1942, she became a junior studio engineer at the BPC."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First All-Electronic Score (1957)
podcast.body: In 1957, Daphne Oram achieved a historical milestone by creating the soundtrack for a play titled "Amphatryon 38," which stands as the first-ever all-electronic score for any production. This groundbreaking work showcased her innovative approach to sound composition. "In 1957, she created the soundtrack for a play called Amphatryon 38, which was the first ever all electronic score for anything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cofundadora y Abandono del BBC Radiofonic Workshop (1958-1959)
podcast.body: Daphne Oram se encargó de poner los pilares de la BBC Radiofonic Workshop, uno de los laboratorios sonoros más importantes de la cultura popular, cuya influencia se extendió a generaciones futuras de músicos electrónicos. Sin embargo, en 1959, Oram abandonó el proyecto que había fundado, ya que estaba más interesada en desarrollar su propia técnica musical y enfoque creativo, lo que la llevó a fundar su propio estudio. "Daphne se encargó de poner los pilares de la que sería una de las fábricas de sonido más importantes de la cultura popular."

srcs.episode: Ellas vieron el futuro: Pioneras de la música electrónica

podcast.title: Fundación de Oramics Studios (1959)
podcast.body: Después de dejar la BBC Radiofonic Workshop en 1959, Daphne Oram fundó Oramics Studios for electronic music and composition. Este estudio es notable por ser el primer estudio de música electrónica creado por una mujer en los años 50, lo que subraya su espíritu pionero y su independencia creativa. "El primer estudio de música electrónica creado por una mujer."

srcs.episode: Ellas vieron el futuro: Pioneras de la música electrónica

podcast.title: Composing with Synthetic Sounds and Esoteric Equipment
podcast.body: After World War II, Oram delved into composing music using synthetic sounds created with esoteric audio equipment such as sine wave oscillators combined with magnetic tape machines. This was before synthesizers were invented, making her studio appear "like something out of a science fiction movie." "So she used things like sine wave oscillators combined with magnetic tape machines."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Desarrollo de la Técnica Oramics (Años 50)
podcast.body: Daphne Oram se centró en desarrollar una técnica innovadora llamada Oramics en su propio estudio. Esta técnica consistía en dibujar directamente sobre película de 35 milímetros; las formas y diseños creados eran luego leídos por células fotoeléctricas y transformados en sonidos, permitiendo una nueva forma de composición musical. "Quería centrarse en orámix, cuando haban guardiista técnica que consistían dibujar directamente sobre película del 35 milímetros."

podcast.title: Early Audio Experimentation
podcast.body: Her wartime role at the BBC led Daphne Oram to experiment extensively with audio recording equipment. After the war, she delved deeply into composing with synthetic sounds, utilizing esoteric audio equipment such as sine wave oscillators combined with magnetic tape recorders, in an era before synthesizers were invented. "This led to her experimenting with audio recording gear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First All-Electronic Score
podcast.body: In 1957, Daphne Oram created the soundtrack for her play titled "Ampatrium 38," marking it as the first-ever all-electronic score for any production. This achievement highlighted her innovative approach to musical composition and laid a foundation for electronic sound in media. "In 1957, she created the soundtrack for her play entitled Ampatrium 38, which was the first ever all electronic score for anything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding BBC Radiophonic Workshop and Own Studio
podcast.body: Daphne Oram was instrumental in convincing the BBC to establish an electronic workshop, which became known as the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, where further experimentation in electronic music ensued. After leaving the BBC in 1959, she founded her own studio, dedicating it to the creation of new and experimental sounds. "Once she convinced the BBC to establish an electronic workshop, they call it the BBC Radio Fonic Workshop, more experimentation followed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding Her Own Studio for New Sounds
podcast.body: After leaving the BBC in 1959, Daphne Oram established her own studio devoted to creating new electronic sounds. Her work there extended to film, where she produced all the electronic sound effects for the first three James Bond movies: "Dr. No," "From Russia with Love," and "Goldfinger," showcasing her unique sonic artistry. "When she left the Beebe in 1959, she founded her own studio devoted to creating new sounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: James Bond Electronic Sounds
podcast.body: Daphne Oram was responsible for creating the distinctive electronic sounds featured in three iconic James Bond movies: "Dr. No," "From Russia with Love," and "Goldfinger." Her unique audio contributions helped define the sonic atmosphere of these early spy thrillers. "For example, the electronic sounds you hear in three James Bond movies, Dr. No from Russia with Love and Goldfinger, were all created by Daphne Oram."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering Electronic Composition
podcast.body: After World War II, Oram deeply explored composing with synthetic sounds, utilizing esoteric audio equipment like sine wave oscillators combined with magnetic tape recorders, as synthesizers had not yet been invented. Her studio was described as resembling something from a science fiction movie. "So she used things like sine wave oscillators combined with magnetic tape recorders. Her studio must have looked like something out of a science fiction movie."

podcast.title: Pioneering Junior Studio Engineer at BBC
podcast.body: In 1942, Daphne Oram began her career at the BBC as a junior studio engineer. Her initial responsibility was to ensure continuous music broadcasts by seamlessly switching to recorded music if transmissions were interrupted by Nazi bombing raids, which sparked her experimentation with audio recording gear. "In 1942, she became a junior studio engineer at the BBC."

xref.title: BBC Radiophonic Workshop Tenure (1962-1973)
xref.body: Delia Derbyshire joined the BBC Radiophonic Workshop in 1962, a facility that Daphne Oram had helped establish. She remained there for 11 years, during which she worked on electronic music for nearly 200 radio and television programs, becoming a pivotal figure in the history of electronic music. "She stayed for 11 years, working on electronic music for close to 200 radio and TV programs using tape machines and oscillators and sine wave generators."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
